title: Exercise for early memory problems
description: Mild cognitive impairment means memory or thinking problems that are noticeable but do not yet interfere much with daily life; it raises the risk of Alzheimer's disease, but not everyone with it goes on to develop dementia. Two separate trials looked at regular aerobic exercise, shown one after the other. In the first, the hippocampus kept its volume better over six months than with balance and toning exercises. In the second, raised blood flow in the left insula was no longer different from people without memory problems after twelve weeks of treadmill walking, and blood flow in two frontal areas fell. Each phase says what brightness means.
caveat: These are studies of mild cognitive impairment, not of Alzheimer's disease itself, and they do not show that exercise prevents or slows Alzheimer's. The first trial included 86 women aged 70 to 80, of whom only 29 had brain scans both before and after; in the exercise group the hippocampus did not grow, it was maintained, and a larger left hippocampus went, unexpectedly, with worse performance on one memory measure. The second study had blood-flow data for 15 people with mild cognitive impairment and 17 without, and no group that did not exercise. The left anterior cingulate is drawn on the pregenual cingulate and the right inferior frontal gyrus on the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, both approximations. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Hippocampus: six months of training
phases.caption: First trial: twice-weekly aerobic training for six months, compared with balance and toning exercises. Afterwards, the hippocampus was larger in the aerobic group than in the comparison group, because it held its size rather than grew. Brightness here is the difference from the comparison group.

phases.name: Blood flow: before exercise
phases.caption: Second study: before exercise, people with mild cognitive impairment had more blood flow in the left insula than people without memory problems. Brightness here is blood flow compared with people without memory problems.

order.rationale: This is a separate study from the first phase; it is shown afterwards only to present the two trials one at a time.

phases.name: Blood flow: after twelve weeks
phases.caption: After twelve weeks of treadmill walking four times a week, the insula difference was no longer present, and blood flow in the left anterior cingulate and the right inferior frontal gyrus had fallen. Brightness here is the change since before exercise.

phases.name: What stayed the same
phases.caption: The hippocampus was maintained, not enlarged, and a bigger one did not mean better memory. The blood-flow study had no group that did not exercise. Neither study shows that exercise prevents Alzheimer's disease.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: Larger on both sides after six months of aerobic training than after balance and toning exercises, in a trial of older women with mild cognitive impairment; within the aerobic group it did not grow, it was maintained. A larger left hippocampus went with worse performance on one memory measure. Brightness stands for the volume difference from the comparison group.
